results.bound: $O(n\log^2 n)$ comparisons, $O(\log n)$ rounds, $4$-approximate sorting, success probability $>1-\frac{1}{n^2}$
results.previous_best: $O(n\log n)$ expected comparisons for 2-approximate sorting vs. non-adaptive adversary [AFJ+18]; deterministic $O(4^k n^{1+1/2^{k-1}})$ and $\Omega(n^{1+1/2^{k-1}})$ [AFHN15]
results.quote: There exists a randomized algorithm that takes $O(n\log^2 n)$ comparisons, uses $O(\log n)$ parallel rounds, and returns a $4$-approximate sorting with probability $>1-\frac{1}{n^2}$.

results.bound: $O(n\log n)$ comparisons, $O(\log n)$ rounds, $4$-approximate $i$-selection, success probability $>1-\frac{1}{n^2}$
results.previous_best: $O(n)$ expected comparisons for 2-approximate selection vs. non-adaptive adversary [AFJ+18]; deterministic $\Omega(n^{9/8})$ lower bound [AFHN15]
results.quote: For any $i$, there exists a randomized algorithm that takes $O(n\log n)$ comparisons, uses $O(\log n)$ parallel rounds, and returns a $4$-approximate $i$-selection with probability $>1-\frac{1}{n^2}$.

results.previous_best: deterministic $k$-approximate sorting: $\Omega(n^{1-1/(2^k-1)})$ rounds and $O(4^k n^{1+1/2^{k-1}})$ comparisons [AFHN15], at best $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ rounds
results.quote: For any integer $d>0$, there exists a deterministic algorithm that takes $d$ rounds, uses $n^{1+O(1/d)}d$ comparisons, and returns a $2d$-approximate sorting.

results.previous_best: deterministic $k$-approximate sorting: $\Omega(n^{1-1/(2^k-1)})$ rounds and $O(4^k n^{1+1/2^{k-1}})$ comparisons [AFHN15], at best $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ rounds
results.quote: For any integer $d>0$, there exists a deterministic algorithm that takes $d$ rounds, uses $n^{1+2/\sqrt{d}}d$ comparisons, and returns a $2d$-approximate sorting.

results.bound: $d+O(\log d)$ rounds, $n^{1+O(1/d)}d\log n$ comparisons, $202$-approximate $i$-selection, success probability $>1-\frac{1}{n^2}$
results.previous_best: deterministic selection: $\Omega(n^{1-1/(2^k-1)})=\Omega(n^{2/3})$ rounds [AFHN15]; deterministic lower bound $\Omega(n^{1+\varepsilon})$
results.quote: For any integer $d>1$ and $i$, there exists a randomized algorithm that takes $d+O(\log d)$ rounds, uses $n^{1+O(1/d)}d\log n$ comparisons, and returns a $202$-approximate $i$-selection with probability $>1-\frac{1}{n^2}$.
